text: In calm times, it worked.
But here's the catch.
Money could only grow as fast as the gold pile,
and in a panic, everyone wants their gold back at the same moment.
There's never enough for everyone at once.
So in emergencies, especially wars, countries kept suspending the link.
Britain cut it for good in 1931.
America went further.
On April 5, 1933, in the depths of the Great Depression,
president Franklin Roosevelt signed executive order 6102. Americans had to
hand most of their gold coins, bars, and gold certificates to the banking system
by May 1st at $20.67 an ounce. Hoard it and you risked a $10,000
fine up to 10 years in prison or both. Imagine explaining that one at a dinner
party. A year later the official price jumped to $35 an ounce. Same gold but
each dollar now stood for about 41 percent less of it, and Americans couldn't legally
own gold bars again until the last day of 1974.
So ordinary people were locked out of gold, but foreign governments weren't, and that
loophole is what eventually broke the whole system.
July 1944, the Second World War is still raging, and delegates from 44 countries check into
a hotel in Bretton Woods, New Hampshire.
Not for a holiday.
The plan, other currencies pegged to the dollar, and the dollar pegs to gold at $35 an ounce,
swappable by foreign governments. Why the dollar? Because at the start, America held
about three quarters of the world's official gold. Suddenly the dollar was as good as gold,
and better in one way. You could invest dollars, gold just sits there looking expensive.
But there was a trap built in. To give the world enough dollars, America had to keep
sending them abroad, and the more dollars piled up overseas, the less the gold in American
vaults could cover them. Economists call this the Triffin Dilemma.
France noticed. In January 1965, it announced it would swap at least $300 million of its
dollars for American gold. Its finance minister, Valerie Giscard-Desteng, called America's
position an exorbitant privilege. America plugged the leaks with a shared gold pool
in London and emergency swaps between central banks. In 1968, the gold pool collapsed.
